sa1:0.3: Translated by the Indian Tripiṭa Guṇabhadra during the [Liu] Song dynasty (ca. 435–443)
sa1:0.5: 1-4 (1). Impermanent, Painful, Empty, and Not Self
sa1:1.2: One time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Jeta’s Grove of Śrāvastī.
sa1:2.1: It was then that the Bhagavān addressed the monks,
sa1:2.2: “You should observe that form is [1] impermanent … [2] painful … [3] empty … [4] not self.
sa1:2.3: Observing it in this way is right view.
sa1:2.4: Correctly observing it gives rise to disillusionment.
sa1:2.5: When someone is disillusioned, delight and greed end.
sa1:2.6: When delight and greed end, I say one’s mind is liberated.
sa1:3.1: “Thus observe that feeling … conception … volition … awareness is [1] impermanent … [2] painful … [3] empty … [4] not self.
sa1:3.2: Observing it in this way is right view.
sa1:3.3: Correctly observing it gives rise to disillusionment.
sa1:3.4: When someone is disillusioned, delight and greed end.
sa1:3.5: When delight and greed end, I say one’s mind is liberated.
sa1:4.1: “In this way, monks, someone who wants to realize the mind’s liberation for themselves can realize:
sa1:4.2: ‘My births have been ended, the religious practice has been established, and the task has been accomplished.’
sa1:4.3: They themselves know they won’t be subject to a later existence.”
sa1:5.1: (Like “observe … impermanent,” “pain,” “emptiness,” and “not self” are taught in the same way.)
sa1:6.1: When the monks heard what the Buddha taught, they rejoiced and approved.
